tagline.general: Pick a measurement of the Earth, watch up to 25 years of it at one place, and see whether it has changed.
tagline.expert: Pick an Earth-system variable, follow up to 25 years of it at one place, and see whether its trend is statistically significant.

card.tourHint: A data companion walks you through four questions: what is changing, where, how much, and whether it is significant.

particles.text: The particles of a layer show one value: the selected place, in the month shown. More, larger or faster particles mean a higher value for that place. They are not a map, and their flow direction is only illustrative.

trend.text: How much the value changes per decade, after removing the normal seasonal cycle. Research mode adds the 95% confidence interval.

marks.text: ▲ rising and ▼ falling: the change holds up in the statistical tests. Hollow △ ▽: weak evidence (it passes the basic test, not the stricter one). ◇: no clear change in this record.

unreliable.text: The test finds a change, but the data itself has a documented problem, such as a jump when the product changed. Do not read it as a climate signal; open its caution note.

notSignificant.text: No clear change (not significant) is not the same as no change. The record may be too short or too noisy to tell.

dataKinds.text: In situ: measured by an instrument at the place. Satellite: worked out from what a sensor in orbit sees. Model: computed by a model that combines observations with physics. They are different kinds of evidence.

cautions.text: An orange note marks a documented problem with a record. Open Details for the numbers and sources.

roles.text: Everyone and Student use plain words; Student adds definitions and reading tips. Researcher shows every statistic and its term. All three show the same numbers.

tour.keys: Enter or → next · ← back · Esc skip
tour.noPlace: The tour needs a single place. Pick one in the Layers panel.
tour.welcome: Hi, I'm Rain. Let me show you how to answer four questions with NASA Earth data: what is changing, where, how much, and whether the change is significant.
tour.particles: This is {{place}} in {{month}}. The particles show one number per layer for this place and month; they are not a map.
tour.particlesCalm: This is {{place}} in {{month}}. The cluster above the place shows one number per layer for this month; it is not a map.

what.tab: Tab ① shows my whole record month by month, and my usual cycle through the year. Other measurements of the same group are listed there too.

where.tab: Tab ② shows the same measurement at many places side by side. Click a box to go to that place.
where.city: Now we are at {{place}}, and the globe turned to it. To see the change at every point on Earth, open Global trend map at the top.

anomaly.general: Tab ③ first takes away the usual yearly cycle, so each month shows how far it was from normal. The trend line turns that into a change per decade.
anomaly.expert: Tab ③ works on monthly anomalies (seasonal cycle removed) and gives the least-squares slope per decade. The table adds its 95% confidence interval and p value.

play.general: The bar on the line centred on 0 is the range the change per decade most likely lies in (95%); if it crosses 0, the direction is not settled. Press play and the cursor moves along the chart with the timeline.
play.expert: The interval plot shows the OLS and Sen slopes with their 95% confidence intervals on a line centred on 0. While the timeline plays, the cursor follows it on the chart.

tests.general: Tab ④ runs two different tests on the record, and each light shows whether that test finds a change. When both agree, the answer is clearer.
tests.expert: Tab ④ shows the OLS t-test (lag-1 autocorrelation corrected) and Mann-Kendall, with p and FDR-adjusted q values. It says whether the two agree.

significant.notSignificant: “Not significant” does not mean “no change”. Often the record is just too short or too noisy to tell.
significant.caveat: Some records have a documented data problem, such as a jump when the product changed. Their trend gets a striped mark and a note: not reliable as a climate signal.

tour.outro: Now it's your turn: try one of these, or jump to any chapter with the numbers above. Reopen me any time with the ? Guide button.
tour.nextResearcher: Switch to Researcher for the full statistics
